```{r setup-knitr, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

A prediction curve needs a set of covariate values at which to evaluate the
model. For example, to plot a treatment group's response to concentration,
we vary concentration and hold the treatment and other covariates fixed.
`data_slice()` creates this prediction grid, called a *data slice*, from a
fitted model or a data frame.

This article builds grids for treatment comparisons and for curves through a
two-dimensional smooth. We load {gratia} for prediction grids, {mgcv} for model
fitting, {dplyr} and {forcats} for data preparation, and {ggplot2} for plotting.

```{r load-packages, results = "hide"}
library("gratia")
library("mgcv")
library("dplyr")
library("ggplot2")
library("forcats")
library("datasets")
```

## Predict uptake for selected plant groups

The `CO2` data from {datasets} record uptake at seven carbon dioxide
concentrations for each of twelve grass plants from Quebec and Mississippi.
The plants received either a chilled or nonchilled treatment. We rename the grouping
variables and make the plant identifier an unordered factor for modelling.

```{r load-co2}
## data load and prep
data(CO2, package = "datasets")
plant <- CO2 |>
  as_tibble() |>
  rename(plant = Plant, type = Type, treatment = Treatment) |>
  mutate(plant = factor(plant, ordered = FALSE))
```

Plot the measurements by origin and treatment to see the curves we want to
predict. Uptake is measured in micromoles per square metre per second and
concentration in microlitres per litre ($\mu\mathrm{L}\,\mathrm{L}^{-1}$).
See Table 1 in the [original study](https://biology.mcgill.ca/faculty/potvin/articles/PotvinLech_90.pdf).

```{r plot-plant-data}
plant_ylab <- expression(CO[2] ~ uptake ~ (mu * mol ~ m^{-2} ~ s^{-1}))
plant_xlab <- expression(CO[2] ~ concentration ~ (mu * L ~ L^{-1}))

plant |>
  ggplot(
    aes(x = conc, y = uptake, group = plant, colour = treatment)
  ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~type) +
  labs(y = plant_ylab, x = plant_xlab, colour = "Treatment")
```

Fit a separate concentration smooth for each combination of treatment and
origin. `tt` identifies those combinations. The plant random intercept allows
each plant to have a different overall uptake level and accounts for dependence
between measurements on the same plant. The Gamma family models a positive,
continuous response, and the log link keeps the fitted mean positive.
```{r fit-plant-gam}
plant <- plant |>
  mutate(tt = fct_cross(treatment, type))
m_plant <- gam(
  uptake ~ treatment * type + s(conc, by = tt, k = 6) +
    s(plant, bs = "re"),
  data = plant, method = "REML", family = Gamma(link = "log")
)
overview(m_plant)
```

Plot the smooth contributions on common scales to compare their shapes. The
panels show contributions to the log of mean uptake. Partial residuals add the
model's weighted working residuals to each smooth, making it easier to see
where the data depart from the fitted curve. We use {patchwork} to collect the
legend in the empty lower-right panel.
```{r draw-plant-model, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 8}
draw(
  m_plant, residuals = TRUE, scales = "fixed",
  ncol = 3, guides = "collect"
) +
  patchwork::guide_area()
```

To predict uptake for chilled Quebec plants, vary `conc` over 100 evenly
spaced values and fix `type` and `treatment`. Unspecified predictors receive
representative values. First inspect this grid to see what that means for
the derived factor `tt`.
```{r plant-ds-1}
ds1 <- data_slice(
  m_plant,
  conc = evenly(conc, n = 100),
  type = level(type, "Quebec"),
  treatment = level(treatment, "chilled")
)
ds1
```

`data_slice()` uses the most common level for an unspecified factor, with
ties resolved by choosing the first tied level. It treats `tt` as a separate
factor, so supply the level that matches `treatment` and `type` before using
this grid for prediction.
```{r plant-ds-1a}
ds1 <- data_slice(
  m_plant,
  conc = evenly(conc, n = 100),
  treatment = level(treatment, "chilled"), type = level(type, "Quebec"),
  tt = level(tt, "chilled:Quebec")
)
ds1
```

Pass the grid to `fitted_values()` for predictions and credible intervals for
mean uptake with the plant random intercept set to zero.
```{r plant-fitted-1}
fv1 <- fitted_values(
  m_plant,
  data = ds1,
  scale = "response",
  exclude = "s(plant)"
)
fv1
```

`exclude` removes the random intercept's contribution even though the grid
contains a plant identifier. With the default `scale = "response"`, the fitted
values and intervals are in uptake units. With a log link, setting the random
intercept to zero gives a prediction for a plant at that reference level.
Averaging over the distribution of plant effects would give a different mean.

Plot that curve and interval alongside the observed measurements for chilled
Quebec plants. The observations include variation between individual plants,
while the curve holds the plant-specific intercept at zero.
```{r plot-plant-fitted-1}
fv1 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = conc, y = .fitted)) +
  geom_point(
    data = plant |>
      filter(type == "Quebec", treatment == "chilled"),
    mapping = aes(y = uptake),
    alpha = 0.8, colour = "steelblue"
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(ymin = .lower_ci, ymax = .upper_ci),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    x = plant_xlab, y = plant_ylab,
    title = expression(Estimated ~ CO[2] ~ uptake),
    subtitle = "Chilled plants of the Quebec type"
  )
```

## Compare treatments on the same concentration grid

To compare treatments for Mississippi plants, request all treatment levels
and one origin. Recreate `tt` from those values so that each prediction row
selects the appropriate smooth.
```{r plant-data-slice-2}
ds2 <- data_slice(
  m_plant,
  conc = evenly(conc, n = 100),
  treatment = evenly(treatment),
  type = level(type, "Mississippi")
) |>
  mutate(
    tt = fct_cross(treatment, type, keep_empty = TRUE)
  )
ds2
```

`fct_cross()` replaces the automatically chosen `tt` value with the correct
treatment-origin combination. `keep_empty = TRUE` retains the factor levels
used when fitting, including combinations absent from this prediction grid.

Predict both treatment curves with the plant-specific intercept set to zero,
then overlay the measurements for Mississippi plants.
```{r draw-plant-fitted-values-2}
fitted_values(
  m_plant,
  data = ds2, scale = "response",
  exclude = "s(plant)"
) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(x = conc, y = .fitted, group = treatment)
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = plant |> filter(type == "Mississippi"),
    mapping = aes(y = uptake, colour = treatment),
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(ymin = .lower_ci, ymax = .upper_ci, fill = treatment),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(colour = treatment)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = plant_xlab,
    y = plant_ylab,
    title = expression(Estimated ~ CO[2] ~ uptake),
    subtitle = "Comparison of treatment in plants of the Mississippi type",
    colour = "Treatment",
    fill = "Treatment"
  )
```

## Choose values for a prediction grid

Use these helpers to select numeric values or factor levels for a grid.

* `evenly(x, n = 100)` returns 100 evenly spaced values from the minimum to the maximum of `x`.
* `evenly(x, by = 5)` takes steps of 5 from the minimum of `x` up to its maximum.
* Supply `lower`, `upper` or both to use different bounds, as in `evenly(x, n = 100, lower = 5, upper = 10)`.
* `evenly(fct)` and `all_levels(fct)` return each level of `fct` once.
* `ref_level(fct)` returns the first level of `fct`. For an unordered factor, this is the reference under R's default contrasts.
* `level(fct, "B")` returns the requested level `"B"`.

Factor helpers preserve the levels used in the fitted model, so a prediction
grid uses the same coding as the fitting data.

`data_slice()` also accepts named R expressions, evaluated using variables
from the fitted model's data or from supplied `data`. Here we select the
lower quartile, median and upper quartile of concentration. Other covariates
retain their representative values.

```{r data-slice-expressions}
data_slice(
  m_plant,
  conc = quantile(conc, probs = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75))
)
```

When several variables have multiple requested values, the grid contains
every combination of those values.

## Keep prediction ranges within each group

When a covariate has a different observed range in each group, a grid spanning
the full range can lead to extrapolation for some groups. Use `.by` to evaluate
expressions separately within each observed group. Here the range of `x` differs
between groups A and B.

```{r grouped-data-slice}
group_data <- data.frame(
  x = c(0, 4, 10, 5, 12, 20),
  fac = factor(rep(c("A", "B"), each = 3)),
  z = c(1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 9)
)
data_slice(
  group_data,
  x = evenly(x, n = 5),
  .by = fac
)
```

This generates five values from 0 to 10 for A, and five from 5 to 20 for B.
The same syntax works for a fitted GAM containing `s(x, by = fac)`. Grouping
variables are included automatically, and only observed groups are used.
Select multiple grouping variables with `.by = c(site, treatment)` to work
within their observed combinations.

Use `fac = level(fac, "B")` to create a grid for B alone. With `.by = fac`,
`data_slice()` selects B before evaluating `evenly(x, n = 5)`, so it uses
that group's range of 5 to 20.

```{r selected-group-data-slice}
data_slice(group_data,
  x = evenly(x, n = 5), fac = level(fac, "B"), .by = fac
)
```

Unspecified covariates, such as `z` above, keep their overall representative
values. To use group-specific values, supply an expression explicitly:

```{r group-specific-reference-value}
data_slice(group_data, x = evenly(x, n = 5), z = mean(z), .by = fac)
```

The returned tibble is ungrouped and preserves the original factor levels and
their ordered status.

With several continuous predictors, a combination can be unobserved even
when each value is within its group's range. Set `.observed_only = TRUE` to
retain only combinations of the specified covariates that occur in the data.
This also removes interpolated points, so leave it off to draw a continuous
curve and check that the chosen grid is supported by observations.

## Plot curves through a two-dimensional smooth

For a surface depending on `x` and `z`, we can plot how the smooth changes
with `x` at selected values of `z`. We simulate a mean surface with two peaks
and sample `x` and `z` independently and uniformly between zero and one.
The response adds independent Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.25.

```{r bivariate-data}
# simulate data from the bivariate surface
df <- data_sim("eg2", n = 1000, scale = 0.25, seed = 2)
```

Fit a tensor product smooth to estimate the surface. We will then evaluate
it along `x` at selected values of `z`.

```{r data-sim-and-fit}
# fit the GAM
m_biv <- gam(y ~ te(x, z), data = df, method = "REML")
```

We will use the same grids to compare smooth contributions from
`smooth_estimates()` with full fitted means from `fitted_values()`.

### Using `smooth_estimates()`

Create a grid over `x` with `z` fixed at its lower quartile. The axis label
records that fixed value so the resulting curve is easy to identify.
```{r data-slice-biv-1}
ds3 <- data_slice(m_biv,
  x = evenly(x, n = 100),
  z = quantile(z, probs = 0.25)
)

z_val <- with(ds3, round(quantile(z, probs = 0.25), 2))
ylab <- bquote(hat(f)(x, .(z_val)))
```

Evaluate the smooth on the grid and add pointwise credible intervals.
```{r smooth-estimates-bivar}
sm <- smooth_estimates(m_biv, select = "te(x,z)", data = ds3) |>
  add_confint()
sm
```

Use ggplot2 to plot the estimated curve and its intervals.
```{r plot-smooth-estimates-bivar}
sm |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = .estimate)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .lower_ci, ymax = .upper_ci), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Evaluation of smooth te(x,z) at fixed z",
    y = ylab
  )
```

With `overall_uncertainty = TRUE`, the default, the interval includes
uncertainty in the intercept even though the plotted estimate is the centred
smooth contribution. Set `overall_uncertainty = FALSE` to base the interval
only on uncertainty in the smooth's coefficients.

To compare curves at low, middle and high values of `z`, request its lower
quartile, median and upper quartile. Each value gets a separate colour and
interval ribbon.
```{r data-slice-biv-2}
ds4 <- data_slice(m_biv,
  x = evenly(x, n = 100),
  z = round(quantile(z, probs = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75)), 2)
)

sm <- smooth_estimates(m_biv, select = "te(x,z)", data = ds4) |>
  add_confint() |>
  mutate(fz = factor(z))

sm |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = .estimate, colour = fz, group = fz)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .lower_ci, ymax = .upper_ci, fill = fz, colour = NULL),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Evaluation of smooth te(x,z) at fixed z",
    y = expression(hat(f)(x, z)), colour = "z", fill = "z"
  )
```

### Using `fitted_values()`

`fitted_values()` evaluates the full model on the grid. For this Gaussian
identity-link model, the fitted mean at each row is the intercept plus the
smooth contribution. The interval quantifies uncertainty in that mean.

We first plot the fitted mean over `x` at the single fixed value of `z`.
```{r data-slice-biv-1-fitted-values}
fitted_values(m_biv, data = ds3) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = .fitted)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .lower_ci, ymax = .upper_ci), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Fitted values from model",
    y = expression(hat(y))
  )
```

We then plot the fitted mean at each of the three fixed values of `z`.
```{r data-slice-biv-2-fitted-values}
fitted_values(m_biv, data = ds4) |>
  mutate(fz = factor(z)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = .fitted, colour = fz, group = fz)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .lower_ci, ymax = .upper_ci, fill = fz, colour = NULL),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Fitted values from model",
    y = expression(hat(y)), colour = "z", fill = "z"
  )
```
